title: Order reservation database waits

sources.claim: Applications borrow and return pooled connections; client pool bounds and Cloud SQL's overall connection limits are separate constraints. An exhausted application pool is not by itself proof of a database connection-limit rejection.

Query Insights distinguishes CPU, IO and lock wait load. By default it represents completed queries unless active-query monitoring is used; the fixture's owner extract supplies active blocking evidence separately.

Active-query diagnostics expose wait events and transaction duration. Blocking analysis and session termination have separate prerequisites and permissions; a supplied observation does not grant the candidate database execution or intervention authority.

cloudsql_database identifies an instance with project_id, database_id and region labels. Application pool and owner diagnostic extracts in this fixture are labelled supplied records, not claimed native Cloud SQL log fields.

a.conclusion: The observed pool bound of two connections throttles this workload before database execution. Two continuously leased connections with roughly 250-ms work support about eight completions per second against twenty incoming requests per second. The authenticated successful connection, session headroom and sampled absence of blocking do not support a connectivity, authentication, database connection-limit or lock-chain diagnosis.
next_checks: The application owner verifies why the effective maximum changed from 20 to 2 and compares admitted concurrency with the request workload.
The application and database owners establish safe aggregate connection headroom before proposing any approved pool adjustment.
Avery continues watching acquisition waits and completed order outcomes; timeout alone does not authorize retrying order effects.
unsupported: Claiming a blocking transaction or database outage despite the supplied pool and database observations.
Calling this a database max_connections breach or prescribing an unlimited pool.
Running SQL, killing sessions, editing the pool, or claiming the candidate executed the supplied connection observation.
unknowns: The source of the effective pool configuration and the safe aggregate connection allocation.
Whether timed-out requests have effects and the state after the supplied window.

b.conclusion: The database is reachable and authentication succeeds, but order-reservation statements wait behind an open transaction. Their retained connections explain secondary application-pool waits; increasing the pool is not a demonstrated cause repair.
next_checks: The database owner and application owner identify backend 701's transaction origin, lock relationships and effect state using their authorized diagnostic process.
Only the owning humans decide whether to let the transaction finish, interrupt it or change application behavior after evaluating rollback and duplicate-effect risks.
Avery correlates blocked statements, pool wait and completed order outcomes after any approved action; an unrelated successful read does not prove recovery.
unsupported: Diagnosing insufficient configured pool size as the primary mechanism while ignoring the demonstrated blocking chain.
Treating RUNNABLE, moderate CPU or one successful read as proof the affected database execution path is healthy.
Terminating backend 701, issuing SQL, raising connection limits or blindly retrying timed-out orders.
unknowns: Why the transaction remains open and whether interrupting it is safe.
The complete set of affected order effects and any sustained recovery after 13:30 UTC.
